1.pericope_label: Moreover the word of the Lord came unto me, saying, Also, thou son of man, thus saith the Lord God unto the land of Israel; An end, the end is come upon the four corners of the land
debates: Why the prophet repeats himself so much
What the four corners of the land means
Whether the received text of the opening cry is sound
outliers: Clarke prefers a manuscript reading supported by all the ancient versions, the end cometh, come is the end, against the received text, and reports that a later hand cancelled a word in his oldest copy to make it agree with the received tradition
Ellicott denies that the four corners rests on any belief that the earth was square, deriving it instead from the many common things that had four sides
Calvin answers the charge of verbosity by arguing that a people perverse in disposition would have found a short command cold and ineffectual
themes: A prophecy sent twice because once would be forgotten
A town crier who does not stop for fine words
An end that comes slowly and comes surely
A cancelled word still discernible under the correction

3.pericope_label: Now is the end come upon thee, and I will send mine anger upon thee, and will judge thee according to thy ways, and will recompense upon thee all thine abominations
debates: Whether the text reads an only evil or evil after evil
What the rare word rendered morning means
Whether the sounding of the mountains is an echo or a real cry
outliers: Clarke finds a play on words joining the root that means to cut off, the one that means to awake from sleep, and the noun for summer, and personifies the end as an executioner risen early and waiting for orders
Calvin calls subtle and unsatisfactory the reading that makes a single evil severe enough to finish the work at one stroke, preferring an unbroken succession of evils
Gill reports the Targum reading that makes the rare word a crowned head, the king of Babylon, which Calvin rejects as distorted
themes: A people who always kept some corner to fly to
An executioner awake before the household
Mercy repelled and then found shut
A harvest shout replaced by the noise of war

10.pericope_label: Behold the day, behold, it is come: the morning is gone forth; the rod hath blossomed, pride hath budded. Violence is risen up into a rod of wickedness
debates: Whether the rod is the foreign conqueror or the guilty nation
What the rare word rendered wailing means
Why the buyer is told not to rejoice
outliers: Ellicott takes rod and tribe as the same word and reads a play upon it, so that where the rod of Aaron budded in evidence of his choosing, the rod standing for the tribe at Jerusalem has budded to its own destruction
Clarke reports that Houbigant, who rarely admits himself puzzled, is completely nonplussed here, and that Calmet offers no fewer than five interpretations of the verse
Calvin distinguishes the general doctrine that the pious pass through the world as pilgrims from the prophet meaning, which is a ruin so total that money and lands have no use at all
themes: A rod grown abroad from a root at home
A husbandman who waits for the tree to reach its height
Mourning that stops when the dead are too many
A bargain neither party will keep

13.pericope_label: For the seller shall not return to that which is sold, although they were yet alive: for the vision is touching the whole multitude thereof, which shall not return
debates: How the year of jubilee bears on the sale of land
Whether the vision not returning means unrepentance or certain effect
Whether the trumpet is blown or commanded to be blown
outliers: Calvin reconciles this with the command that a prophet buy a field while in prison, saying that purchase was for the faithful who might wait for restitution with quiet minds, while this discourse is aimed at those shut out from all hope
Ellicott quotes Jerome, that it is natural to rejoice in a purchase and mourn over a sale, but when slavery and captivity stare a man in the face, rejoicing and mourning are equally absurd
Gill records a reading followed by the Septuagint and the Arabic version that turns the trumpet into a command, which he would take as sarcasm
themes: A year of release that arrives while its heirs are abroad
A prophecy that cannot come back empty
An alarm sounded to an army that will not march
A door shut against an enemy that is already inside

16.pericope_label: But they that escape of them shall escape, and shall be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them mourning, every one for his iniquity
debates: Whether escape contradicts the wrath pronounced on all
Whether the mourning is repentance or only punishment
Whether sackcloth and baldness are signs of penitence
outliers: Calvin answers that the survivors fare worse than the slain, because in dry and desert places they dare not cry out, and the wretch who dares not complain is twice dead among the living
Ellicott takes iniquity here to mean the punishment of iniquity and says repentance is not in view, while Wesley leaves both senses open
Clarke reports that Calmet and Jerome read the watery knees as the loss of bodily control under terror, and says he believes them nearly right
themes: Lions of the mountains turned into doves of the valleys
A survivor who may not even weep aloud
A mourning sign the law itself had forbidden
A guilty conscience carried into the hills

19.pericope_label: They shall cast their silver in the streets, and their gold shall be removed: their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the Lord
debates: Whether the beauty of the ornament is the temple or the peoples wealth
What the strong word applied to their gold means
Whether the secret place is the holy of holies or the land itself
outliers: Calvin refuses the temple reading on the ground that the prophet explains his own words by naming gold and silver, and Ellicott agrees, taking every pronoun in the verse to refer to the people
Gill reports Kimchi that the silver and gold cast away may be their idols of silver and gold, now held in contempt for failing to save them
Calvin draws from the plundering a general rule, that abandoned men are the scourges of God and governed by his hand, yet he is pure from all alliance with their faults
themes: A pound of gold not worth an ounce of bread
A soldier shedding treasure to run faster
A gift turned first to pride and then into an idol
A face turned away that neither helps nor restrains

23.pericope_label: Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence. Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses
debates: Whether the chain means captivity or arraignment
In what sense the heathen brought are the worst
Why the sanctuary is called their holy places and not his
outliers: Calvin sets himself against the interpreters who refer the chain to exile, taking it instead of criminals who plead their cause in chains, already as it were half condemned
Ellicott refers worst to the power and thoroughness of the invaders work rather than to their character, against Gill and Clarke who take it morally
Calvin holds that the impious cannot move a finger but by God will, and yet that he has nothing in common with them, since they are carried by a depraved impulse
themes: A chain that drags a prisoner to the bar
A faithful city turned harlot
A scourge kept for the fire once its work is done
A shield held up against the one who gave it

26.pericope_label: Mischief shall come upon mischief, and rumour shall be upon rumour; then shall they seek a vision of the prophet; but the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the ancients
debates: Whether the king and the prince are the same person
Whether the clause denies that any prophet will be found
Why the removal of counsel is the heaviest part of the judgment
outliers: Gill takes king and prince as one and the same, naming Zedekiah, while Wesley keeps the king as Zedekiah but reads the prince of every magistrate

Calvin finds the clause about seeking a vision too abrupt and considers reading a particle negatively, so that the prophet denies there will be any prophets, admitting the language may not properly bear it
Clarke observes that before great national judgments God restrains the influences of his Spirit, so that statesmen devise foolish schemes and hasten the ruin they meant to avert
themes: A debtor who pays a little and grows careless again
Three doors of counsel knocked at and none opening
A chart of guidance withdrawn mid-voyage
Shame given as a garment to the elders
